why_how.text: Grade crossings count as intersections where a train can come at any time from either side.
Crossing signals, signs and markings tell you when to stop, and some vehicles must always stop.
A vehicle stalled on the tracks must be emptied at once and the emergency number called.

scenario.text: Lisa reaches a crossing where the red lights are flashing but she cannot see a train.

reasoning.text: Flashing reds, bells or gates command a halt at least fifteen feet short, held until they stop and gates fully rise.

result.text: Lisa stops at least fifteen feet back and waits until the lights stop.

claim.text: Common mistake: driving around a lowered gate when no train is in sight.

correction.text: Skirting gates or flashing reds is illegal and deadly, and you never duck around or under moving gates.

memory_support.text: Expect a train, stop fifteen back, wait for gates up.

prompt.text: Your car stalls on the railroad tracks. What is the first thing to do?

answer.text: Get everyone out of the vehicle immediately.

rationale.text: Then clear the rails without waiting to see a train, and call the number on the emergency sign.

narration.text: This chapter covers special driving conditions that demand sharper attention and judgment: railroad crossings, expressways, night driving, bad weather, and emergencies. We begin with railroad grade crossings. The manual treats a crossing as an intersection, with one big difference: the other traffic is a train that cannot stop quickly. In this lesson we cover how to approach crossings with and without gates, what the warning signs and signals mean and where to stop, which vehicles must always stop, and what to do if your vehicle stalls on the tracks. These rules prevent some of the deadliest crashes on the road.

lines.text: Trains on any track, any time.
Never race gates; never stop on rails.

narration.text: Grade crossings count as intersections, and at every one you should always expect a train, on any track, at any time, from either direction. Never race the gates, and never stop on the rails. When you cross, stay in your lane and keep the car in gear. The manual adds a warning about how trains look: any train you can see is closer, faster and harder to stop than it appears. So the safest assumption is always that a train could be coming, and that you have less time than you think if you do see one approaching the crossing ahead.

lines.text: Active: wait for gates up, lights off.

narration.text: At an active crossing, with gates or flashing lights, you may cross only after the gates have fully risen and the lights have stopped. Driving around gates or past flashing red lights is illegal and deadly. At a passive crossing, with no signals, you slow down, approach ready to stop, confirm the tracks are clear, and where there are several tracks, scan every one of them both ways. The manual sums up the contrast: gated crossings hold you until the bells stop and gates rise, while gateless ones demand your own careful judgment of whether the tracks are clear.

A yellow railroad crossing sign warns that a crossing is ahead. Slow down, be ready to stop, and take care behind buses and trucks that may stop there. Flashing red lights, bells or gates command you to stop at least fifteen feet short of the tracks. Stay stopped until the bells are silent and the gates are fully up, and never go around or under gates that are moving. At gateless crossings, a painted stop line often shows where to wait. So the signals tell you when to stop, and the distance keeps you clear of the train and the gates.

lines.text: Your own look and listen can veto.
Only cross if you can clear it.

narration.text: A crossbuck, the X-shaped sign, orders you to yield and shows how many tracks there are. Your own look-and-listen judgment can overrule a signal: never cross against a train that is near or fast, even if the signals seem dead. Enter a crossing only if you can clear it completely, with room on the other side; if traffic is blocking the far side, wait. School buses with or without passengers, other buses carrying passengers, and vehicles with explosives or flammable cargo must stop at every crossing, so expect them to stop and be ready to stop behind them yourself.

lines.text: Gated: wait for bells and gates.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers treat any crossing the same, or drive around a gate when no train is in sight. The manual draws the line: gated crossings hold drivers until the bells stop and gates fully rise, while gateless ones demand slowed, stop-ready approaches with confirmed-clear tracks. Signaled versus self-judged entries. At a gated crossing the signal decides, and going around it is illegal and deadly. At a gateless crossing, you decide, so you must look and listen carefully. In both cases, any visible train is nearer, faster and less stoppable than it looks.

Here is a quick check: your car stalls on the railroad tracks. What is the first thing to do? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to get everyone out of the vehicle immediately. Then clear the rails, without waiting to see whether a train is coming, and call the number on the posted emergency notification sign. The manual stresses that stalled cars empty every occupant at once, before anything else. If a train is coming, you run toward the train at an angle away from the tracks, which a later lesson explains in more detail.

lines.text: Stop fifteen feet back for signals.

narration.text: To close, grade crossings count as intersections where you always expect a train on any track at any time, never race gates, never rest on the rails, and cross in your lane and in gear. Active crossings release you only after gates fully rise and lights stop. Passive crossings demand a slow, stop-ready approach with every track checked. Flashing reds, bells or gates mean stop at least fifteen feet short. Crossbucks mean yield, and school buses loaded or empty, passenger buses, and explosive or flammable cargo haulers always stop. If you stall, everyone gets out, clears the rails and calls the emergency sign's number. Next come expressways.

why_how.text: Expressways are divided, one-way roads entered and left only by ramps.
Entering and leaving safely depends on matching speeds and planning ahead.

scenario.text: Omar enters an expressway from a short stub lane with no room to speed up.

reasoning.text: Stub lanes stop to await wide gaps before sprinting aboard, unlike full ramps that accelerate for rolling merges.

result.text: Omar stops, waits for a wide gap, then speeds onto the expressway.

claim.text: Common mistake: backing up on a ramp after taking the wrong exit.

correction.text: Expressways forgive wrong exits only via the next exit, and ramp reversing and median crossing are forbidden as deadly.

memory_support.text: Full ramp, roll in; stub lane, stop first.

prompt.text: You took the wrong exit off an expressway. What should you do?

answer.text: Continue to the next exit and correct your route from there.

rationale.text: Never reverse on a ramp or cross the median, which the manual calls deadly.

narration.text: This lesson covers expressways: divided highways with one-way traffic in several lanes, entered and left only by ramps. The manual explains what makes them different, their usual speed limits, and how to plan your entrances and exits. Then it explains how to enter from a full ramp and from a short stub lane, how to change lanes, and how to exit. Finally it covers the extra demands of fast, dense traffic. Driving here requires quicker thinking than ordinary roads, so the habits in this lesson are worth practicing before your first long expressway trip.

An expressway divides traffic into one-way, multi-lane roadways, with access only by ramps. The usual speed limit is fifty-five, with sixty-five on rural stretches of thruways, interstates and parkways. Plan your entrance and exit before you start. If you take the wrong exit, the only fix is to go on to the next exit. Never back up on a ramp or cross the median, which the manual calls deadly. So an expressway rewards planning: know where you will get on and off, and if you miss your exit, keep going and correct your route at the next one.

lines.text: Stub lane: stop, wait for a gap.

narration.text: On a full ramp with no sign telling you otherwise, speed up to match traffic, signal, check over your shoulder, and blend into the lane, slowing if needed. On a short stub lane, stop and wait for a wide gap, then speed up quickly onto the road. Drivers already on the expressway should move out of the right lane to let entering traffic in when they can. The manual's contrast is simple: full ramps accelerate to traffic speed for rolling merges, while stub lanes stop dead to wait for wide gaps, opposite entries for opposite geometry.

lines.text: Read exit signs; move over early.
Signal one hundred feet out; slow down.

narration.text: To change lanes, signal, check over your shoulder, move, and then cancel the signal. To exit, read the signs ahead of time, move into the exit lane early, signal one hundred feet before the exit, and slow to the speed posted for the ramp. After you leave the expressway, check your speedometer, because your sense of speed is tuned to the faster road. Fast, dense traffic also demands quicker thinking, regular rest stops, and sunglasses to cut glare. So the expressway asks for planning at both ends and steady attention in between.

Here is a quick check: you realize you have taken the wrong exit off an expressway. What should you do? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to continue to the next exit and correct your route from there. Never back up on the ramp and never cross the median, which the manual calls deadly. And when you entered, remember the two kinds of entry: on a full ramp you speed up and merge, while on a stub lane you stop and wait for a wide gap before speeding onto the road. Planning ahead avoids most of these problems.

lines.text: Full ramps roll; stub lanes stop.
Signal exits one hundred feet out.

narration.text: To wrap up, expressways divide one-way, multi-lane traffic with ramp access, normally posted at fifty-five with sixty-five on rural thruways, interstates and parkways. Plan your entrances and exits, fix a wrong exit only by taking the next one, and never reverse on a ramp or cross the median. Full ramps speed up to traffic speed for signaled, shoulder-checked merges, while stub lanes stop and wait for wide gaps. Signal and shoulder-check lane changes, signal exits one hundred feet out, slow to the ramp limit, and recheck your speed afterward. Next comes night driving.

why_how.text: Most driving decisions depend on sight, so night driving demands extra caution.
The law sets when headlights must be on and when high beams must be dimmed.

scenario.text: Tia is driving at night with high beams on when a car appears ahead coming toward her.

reasoning.text: Beams drop within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic.

result.text: Tia switches to low beams once the oncoming car is within five hundred feet.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking parking lights or daytime running lights are enough at dusk.

correction.text: Parking and daytime lamps never substitute for headlights, and dawn, dusk and fog always warrant beams for conspicuity.

memory_support.text: Five hundred meeting, two hundred following.

prompt.text: When following another vehicle at night, within what distance must you dim your high beams?

rationale.text: Beams drop within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic and two hundred behind leaders in any lane.

narration.text: This lesson covers driving at night. The manual explains why darkness makes driving harder, why older drivers need to be especially careful, and how fast you can safely drive given the reach of your headlights. Then it sets out when the law requires headlights, including some daytime conditions, and why headlights matter for being seen as well as for seeing. Finally, it gives the rules for dimming high beams for oncoming and leading traffic, how to handle glare from other drivers, and how to set up the inside of your car for night driving.

lines.text: Aging eyes see less at night.

narration.text: The manual says ninety percent of driving decisions depend on sight, so night driving demands extra caution, especially as eyes age and see less well in the dark. On roads that are unfamiliar or twisting, slow down below the speed you would drive in daylight. Your headlights reach about three hundred fifty feet, and your safe speed is one that lets you stop within that distance. So at night, the edge of your headlight beam is the edge of what you can respond to, and your speed should leave you room to stop before you reach it.

lines.text: Half an hour after sunset to before sunrise.

narration.text: The law requires headlights from half an hour after sunset until half an hour before sunrise, whenever visibility is under one thousand feet, and whenever the weather calls for your windshield wipers. At dawn, at dusk and in fog, headlights help other drivers see you, even if you can see well enough without them. Parking lights and daytime running lights never take the place of headlights. And if another driver flashes their lights at you, it may mean yours are off, so switch them on. So headlights are about being seen as much as about seeing.

lines.text: Dim within five hundred feet meeting.
Dim within two hundred feet following.
Look to the right edge if blinded.

narration.text: Dim your high beams within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic, within two hundred feet behind a vehicle you are following in any lane, and for pedestrians walking toward you. If an oncoming driver does not dim, give one brief flash of your high beams, then look toward the right edge of the road and use it as your guide. When others are behind you, use your mirror's night setting. Inside the car, keep the dome light off, dim the dashboard, keep the visor up, and keep the windows clean. All of this cuts glare and helps you see further.

lines.text: Parking and daytime lights never substitute.
Dawn, dusk and fog: headlights on.

narration.text: Here is the trap. At dusk or in light fog, some drivers rely on parking lights or daytime running lights, thinking that is enough. The manual says parking lamps and daytime lamps never substitute for headlights, and that dawn, dusk and fog always warrant headlights, for being seen as well as for seeing. The law also requires headlights whenever visibility drops under one thousand feet and whenever the weather calls for wipers. So if you are unsure, turn on your real headlights. And if another driver flashes their lights at you, take it as a sign to switch yours on.

Here is a quick check: you are driving at night with high beams on, following another vehicle. Within what distance must you dim your high beams? Work it out before reading on. The answer is two hundred feet. For oncoming traffic the distance is five hundred feet, and you also dim for pedestrians coming toward you. If an oncoming driver fails to dim, give a single brief flash, then look to the right edge of the road. And remember that your safe speed at night is one that lets you stop within the reach of your headlights.

lines.text: Headlights at dusk, dawn and low visibility.
Dim at five hundred and two hundred feet.

narration.text: To close, ninety percent of driving decisions ride on sight, so nights demand extra caution, especially as eyes age. Slow below daylight pace on strange or twisting roads, and keep your speed within the roughly three hundred fifty feet your headlights reach. Headlights are required from half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise, in visibility under one thousand feet, and in wiper weather, and parking or daytime lights never substitute. Dim within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic and two hundred feet behind leaders, and keep the cabin dark and the glass clean. Next comes bad weather.

why_how.text: Wet, foggy and icy roads cut traction and visibility.
Skids call for different responses depending on which wheels slide.

scenario.text: Ben's rear wheels start to slide on an icy curve.

reasoning.text: Rear skids steer the travel direction, with anti-lock brakes pressed steadily and plain brakes pumped.

result.text: Ben steers in the direction he wants to travel and brakes steadily with his anti-lock brakes.

claim.text: Common mistake: using high beams in fog to see better.

correction.text: Low beams pierce falling rain, fog and snow that high beams bounce back.

memory_support.text: Low beams in weather; rear skid, steer where you travel.

prompt.text: Which headlights should you use in fog?

rationale.text: High beams bounce back off falling rain, fog and snow, while low beams pierce them.

narration.text: This lesson covers driving in bad weather. Rain, wet leaves, fog and snow cut both your traction and your view, and winter adds ice and snow on the road. The manual explains how to drive on wet roads and avoid hydroplaning, which headlights to use in rain, fog and snow, and when fog lamps may be used. Then it covers getting ready for winter, how different kinds of vehicles behave on slick roads, how to recover from a skid, and how to brake on ice. We will finish by comparing high and low beams, and rear and front skids.

lines.text: Take care on curves and ramps.

narration.text: Wet roads, including roads slick with fallen leaves, call for slower speeds, more space between vehicles, and extra care on curves and ramps. At higher speeds, or with worn or soft tires, your tires can float off the pavement on a film of water. This is hydroplaning, and it means total loss of traction and steering. The manual says hydroplaning punishes haste and rewards deep tread and much slower speeds. So keep your tires in good condition, and when the road is wet, slow down well below your normal speed, especially where water collects.

lines.text: Low beams: five hundred oncoming, two hundred ahead.
Low beams in rain, fog, and snow.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers switch to high beams in fog or heavy rain, thinking more light means better sight. Headlights must be on low beam within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle or within two hundred feet of a vehicle ahead, and kept on low beam in rain, fog, or snow because high beams reflect moisture. So in rain, fog or snow, high beams make things worse, reflecting light into your eyes. Keep headlights on low beam near oncoming or leading vehicles and whenever rain, fog, or snow is falling.

lines.text: Service the car; fit snow tires early.
Never mix radial and bias tires.
Studs: October sixteenth to April thirtieth.

narration.text: Prepare for winter by getting the car serviced early and fitting snow tires. Never mix radial and bias-ply tires on the same vehicle. Studded tires are allowed only from October sixteenth through April thirtieth. In a storm, drive only if you must, and first clear every light, wiper, panel and window, using washer fluid that will not freeze. Drive at the speed conditions allow. The manual notes that rear-wheel-drive cars tend to show a slide coming, while front-wheel and all-wheel-drive cars can feel grippy until they suddenly lose traction.

lines.text: Rear skid: steer the way you travel.

narration.text: In a rear-wheel skid, steer in the direction you want the car to travel, correcting as it swings. With anti-lock brakes, press steadily; with ordinary brakes, pump them, faster as you slow, and never stomp. In a front-wheel skid, lift off the gas, shift to neutral or press the clutch, and hold off steering until the sideways drag restores grip, then steer and ease back on the gas. To prevent skids, brake early and gently, ease off and downshift. And remember that bridges, ramps and overpasses freeze first, and slick patches can linger after the rest of the road clears.

lines.text: Rear: steer into your travel direction.

narration.text: Here is a second trap. People learn one skid rule and apply it to every skid. The manual separates them. Rear-wheel slides steer into the travel direction, with anti-lock brakes pressed steadily or plain brakes pumped faster, while front-wheel slides lift off the gas, shift to neutral, and withhold steering until drag restores grip. So in a rear skid you steer right away, but in a front skid you wait before steering. Knowing which wheels are sliding tells you which response to use, and using the wrong one can make the skid worse.

Here is a quick check: you are driving in fog. Which headlights should you use? Work it out before reading on. The answer is low beams. High beams bounce back off falling rain, fog and snow, while low beams pierce them. When the weather calls for wipers, the law also requires real headlights, not daytime running lights. Approved fog lamps may help too, but only until the skies clear. And if you skid on a slick road, remember the difference: steer into your direction of travel in a rear skid, but wait for grip before steering in a front skid.

lines.text: Low beams and real headlights in weather.

narration.text: To close, wet and leaf-slicked roads demand slower speeds, wider spacing and care on curves and ramps, and hydroplaning can float tires off the pavement at speed or on worn tires. Wiper weather requires real headlights, low beams pierce rain, fog and snow that high beams bounce back, and approved fog lamps run only until the skies clear. Prepare for winter with service and snow tires, never mix radial and bias tires, and use studs only from October sixteenth to April thirtieth. In a rear skid steer the way you travel; in a front skid lift off, shift to neutral and wait for grip. Next come deer and emergencies.

why_how.text: Deer strikes cluster in certain months and hours, so drivers can prepare.
Each vehicle emergency has its own step-by-step response, starting with staying calm.

scenario.text: Raj's brake pedal suddenly sinks to the floor.

reasoning.text: Floor-bound brake pedals invite pumping, then gradual use of the emergency brake plus downshifting.

result.text: Raj pumps the pedal, applies the parking brake gradually and downshifts to slow down.

claim.text: Common mistake: turning off the ignition when the gas pedal sticks.

correction.text: Stuck throttles take neutral and braking without ever killing the ignition, which can lock the steering.

memory_support.text: Brakes fail, pump; steering fails, coast; never panic.

prompt.text: A tire blows out while you are driving. What do you do first?

answer.text: Grip the wheel firmly and ease off the gas.

rationale.text: Brake only once the car is under control, and leave the road when it is safe.

narration.text: This lesson covers deer and vehicle emergencies. The manual explains when and where deer strikes are most likely and how to defend against them. Then it sets out the first rule for every emergency, which is not to panic, followed by specific responses to a tire blowout, steering failure, brake failure, dead headlights, a stuck accelerator, wheels running off the pavement, and a vehicle coming at you head-on. Each emergency has its own steps, and some of them are the opposite of what instinct suggests, so we will compare the brake and steering failures directly.

lines.text: Most strikes in autumn breeding months.
Herds follow leaders; watch signed zones.

narration.text: Deer strikes cluster in the autumn months, October through December, when deer are moving during breeding season, and their activity peaks at dawn and dusk, when commuters are on the road. Deer travel in groups following a leader, so where one crosses, more may follow. Signed deer zones mark areas with heavy strikes. So be most alert at dim hours and in those months, slow down near roadsides and crossings, expect more deer after the first one bolts, flash your lights to warn other drivers, and take posted deer-crossing signs seriously.

lines.text: Blowout: firm grip, ease off gas.

narration.text: Every emergency starts by refusing to panic and taking a second or two to think. A blowout usually announces itself with a thumping sound. Grip the wheel firmly, ease off the gas, handle the car as you would on ice, brake only once it is under control, and leave the road when it is safe. A wheel coming off feels similar; stop and inspect. If your steering fails, take your foot off the gas, turn on your flashers, keep off the brake while the car rolls straight on its momentum, and then brake gently to a stop. Grip, ease off, then brake gently: that is the blowout order.

lines.text: Brake pedal to the floor: pump it.
Stuck throttle: neutral, brake, ignition on.

narration.text: If the brake pedal sinks to the floor, pump it, then use the emergency brake gradually and downshift to slow the car. If your headlights die, try the emergency flashers, parking lights and turn signals so you can see to get off the road; if they dim, get service or stop and get help. If the accelerator sticks, try to hook it up with your shoe; if that fails, shift to neutral, brake and get off the road. Never turn off the ignition, because that can lock the steering, leaving you unable to steer while the car is still moving.

lines.text: Failed brakes: pump, then emergency brake.

narration.text: Here is the trap. People think every emergency calls for hard braking. The manual contrasts two failures. Dead brakes invite pumping, then gradual use of the emergency brake and downshifting, while dead steering invites coasting with the gas off, flashers on and the brake off. Pressure versus patience. With failed brakes, you actively work to slow down. With failed steering, you keep off the brake and let the car roll straight on its momentum, then feather the brake to a stop. Match the response to what has failed.

lines.text: Wheels off the edge: no snap-back.
Ease off, brake gently, check behind.
Head-on threat: slow, go right, honk.

narration.text: If your wheels drop off the edge of the pavement, do not snap back onto the road. Ease off the gas, brake gently, check behind you, and steer back carefully when it is safe. If a vehicle comes at you head-on in your lane, slow down, move to the right and sound your horn. Never swerve to the left, because if the other driver recovers into their own lane, you would meet them head-on there. So for both of these threats, smooth, controlled moves to the right are safer than sudden reactions, and the left lane is the wrong escape route.

Here is a quick check: a tire blows out while you are driving. What do you do first? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to grip the wheel firmly and ease off the gas, handling the car as you would on ice. Brake only once the car is under control, and leave the road when it is safe. Before any of that, the manual says every emergency starts by refusing to panic for a second or two. If your brakes failed instead, you would pump them; if your steering failed, you would coast with the brake off. Panic is the first thing to refuse in every one of these cases.

lines.text: Each failure has its own steps.

narration.text: To close, deer strikes cluster from October through December during breeding travel and peak at dawn and dusk, herds follow leaders, and signed zones mark heavy-hit areas, so slow down and expect more than one deer. Every emergency starts by refusing to panic. In a blowout, grip firmly, ease off the gas and brake only when tame. With steering failure, coast with flashers on and brake off. With brake failure, pump, then use the emergency brake and downshift. With a stuck throttle, shift to neutral and brake, never killing the ignition. Off the pavement, ease back; for a head-on threat, go right.

why_how.text: A car stalled under an approaching train or sinking in water leaves only seconds to act.
Smoke and blocked vision call for getting safely off the road.

scenario.text: Kim's car stalls on the tracks and she sees a train coming.

reasoning.text: Track stalls shed belts and riders and move away toward the train side, at forty-five degrees off the rails.

result.text: Kim gets everyone out and runs toward the train at an angle away from the tracks.

claim.text: Common mistake: running away from the train down the tracks.

correction.text: Escapees run toward the oncoming train at forty-five degrees off the rails, rather than down-track with it, dodging the debris.

memory_support.text: Toward the train, at an angle; windows, not doors.

prompt.text: Your car is in water and still floating. How should you get out?

answer.text: Take your belt off and leave through a window, not a door.

rationale.text: If the car sinks, air pockets near the back seat can help you escape through a window.

narration.text: This last lesson of the chapter covers a few rare but deadly emergencies. The manual explains how to escape a car stalled on the tracks with a train approaching, how to get out of a car that has gone into water, what to do if smoke comes from under the hood, and what to do if something suddenly blocks your view. The steps here are counterintuitive in places, such as which way to run from the tracks and which way to leave a car in water, so it pays to learn them before you ever need them. The chapter then closes with its review questions.

lines.text: Move away toward the train side.
No train in sight: try a restart.

narration.text: If your car stalls on the tracks and a train is coming, take off your seat belt, get everyone out, and move away toward the side the train is coming from. If you are sure the tracks are clear, roll down the windows and listen for a train while you try to restart; if the car will not start, shift to neutral and push it off the tracks. The manual adds a key detail on which way to run: toward the oncoming train, at about forty-five degrees away from the rails, rather than down the tracks in the direction the train is going, to avoid debris from the impact.

lines.text: At an angle off the rails.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Instinct says to run away from a train, down the tracks. The manual says escapees run toward the oncoming train at forty-five degrees off the rails rather than down-track with it, dodging the debris cone of the impact. When the train hits the car, wreckage is thrown forward in the direction the train is moving. So running down the tracks puts you in that path. Running toward the train and off to the side at an angle takes you away from the rails and out of the debris zone at the same time. Toward the train and off at an angle is the whole rule.

lines.text: Belt off; out through a window.
Sunk: air near the back seat.

narration.text: If your car goes into water, it may float briefly. Use that time: take off your seat belt and get out through a window, never a door. If the car has already sunk, there may be air pockets near the back seat. Take a breath there, then escape through a window, breathing out freely as you rise to the surface. So in water, the window is the way out, not the door, and the seconds while the car is still floating are your best chance. Belt off, window open, out: those are the steps in order. The door is the wrong way out of a car in water.

lines.text: Smoke from the hood: pull off.
Ignition off, get away, call fire.

narration.text: If smoke comes from under the hood, pull off the road, turn off the ignition, move away from the car and call the fire department, with no heroics. If something suddenly blocks your view, such as the hood flying up, look out the side window, turn on your flashers and pull off the road to park. The chapter closes with review questions on missed exits, ramps and stub entries, exit signaling and checks, how expressways differ, night driving, headlight range and glare, weather lights, skids, slick braking, emergencies, blowouts, brake failure and getting back onto the pavement.

lines.text: A car in water, still floating.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: your car has gone into water and is still floating. How should you get out? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to take your seat belt off and leave through a window, never a door, using the brief time the car floats. If the car has already sunk, look for air pockets near the back seat, take a breath, and escape through a window, breathing out as you rise. And if your car stalls on the tracks with a train coming, get out and run toward the train at an angle away from the rails. Windows, not doors, and toward the train, not away down the tracks.

lines.text: Run toward the train, at an angle.
Smoke: pull off, get away, call.

narration.text: To wrap up, a track stall with a train coming means belts off, everyone out, and away toward the train side at about forty-five degrees off the rails, not down the tracks, to avoid debris. With no train in sight, listen with windows down while trying a restart, then push the car off in neutral. A car in water should be left through a window during its brief float, never a door, using back-seat air pockets if it sinks. Smoke from the hood means pull off, ignition off, get away and call the fire department. A blocked view means side window, flashers and pull off.
